cite: In re Eddy, 10 Abb. N. Cas. 396
holding_summary: Under the 1875 statute, rent followed ownership during the period in which the property earned it. The receiver could retain only eleven-thirtieths of June's rent, with the remainder belonging to the tenant who purchased the dwelling on June 11.

quotes.text: Prior to June 11,1881, on which day she became the owner thereof by a conveyance from the receiver, Rosina E. Eddy occupied the premises No. 110 West One Hundred and Twenty-third Street, in New York city, as the tenant of James D. Fish, the receiver of the Globe Mutual Life Insurance Company.

By the statute, which reverses the common law rule, the right to the rent follows the ownership of the estate during the period it was earned by the property, and as Mr. Fish had title during eleven days only in the month of June, 1881, he had no right to receive and retain the rent for the entire month, but was entitled to eleven-thirtieths thereof, and the remainder belonged to the new owner, who is the moving party in this proceeding.
This statutory mandate can, of course, only be obeyed by giving to the old and to the new owner of the estate, the proportion which is earned by the property during the ownership of each

notes: Relevant as enforcement and allocation of rent arising from residential occupancy, although the opinion does not disclose the tenancy's total duration.

cite: Jackson v. Odell, 14 Abb. N. Cas. 42
court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: A landlord who knowingly induced a six-month lease through a false representation about the dwelling's condition could not recover the remaining rent if the tenant abandoned within a reasonable time after discovering the fraud. Whether the landlord made such a fraudulent representation was for the jury.

quotes.text: The lease in this case was for six months, from the first of November to the first of May following, the rent being payable montly in advance.

A lessor, who induced the lessee to accept the lease by knowingly making a false representation as to the condition of the premises in response to inquiry by the lessee, cannot recover rent in case the tenant abandons the demised premises within a reasonable time after entry, and as soon as the falsity of the representation becomes apparent.

There was an additional allegation, by way of counter-claim, that the defendant hired the house for the purpose of keeping a boarding-house, but from the causes above stated, it was not suitable for such a purpose, and that the defendant could not, in consequence, secure and keep as many boarders as he otherwise would have been able to have done, to his damage, &c.

If this were the fact, the defendant, upon ascertaining the fraud on the part of the plaintiff, might repudiate the contract,, and if, after remaining there seveveral months, paying rent and repeatedly calling the plaintiff’s attention, to the condition of the house, he became at last thoroughly satisfied of the fraud practiced upon him by the plaintiff—that he would do nothing to repair the wrong he had done and that the defendant by continuing to live in the house was imperiling the life of himself and of his family— he -was justified in quitting the premises

notes: The court treated operation of a boarding house as a legitimate contemplated use and protected the operator from a fraudulently induced lease.

cite: Pomeroy v. Tyler, 9 N.Y. St. Rep. 514
holding_summary: A tenant who leased rooms in an apartment house could not avoid rent merely because the rooms were infested with vermin. In the absence of fraud or an express condition, abandonment did not discharge the tenant's covenant to pay rent.

quotes.text: The action is on a written lease of a' suit of rooms bathe apartment house of the plaintiff, known as the “Four Seasons.”

The hiring was for one year from November 1, 1882, and the recovery sought is the rent from May 1,1883, till October 1,1883. The defendant abandoned the premises-April 30, 1883, having paid the rent during the period of his occupation.

A tenant who hires premises takes them for better or worse. The landlord, in the absence of fraud, or express condition, is not responsible for the presence of rats, mice, bugs or roaches about his premises, and the. fact that the premises are infested by them, constitutes no defense to an. action for the rent.

The tenant choose to move from the premises, he had the right to exercise this privilege, but his abandonment does not reheve him from his obligation to perform the covenants to pay contained in the lease under which he held the premises.

notes: Favorable because the court enforced a compensated furnished-room lease, although the arrangement was an apartment-house tenancy rather than householder lodging.
